1401.title: G-D-L
1401.hook: gadol, gedulah: great, and to grow
1401.howItsDone: The Kaddish, recited in synagogue services and by mourners, begins with yitgadal, from the root G-D-L, asking that God's name grow great; in Jewish speech a gadol can mean a great Torah scholar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, P-Sh-T: peshat, the plain sense, the floor every reading stands on. Today, a new week, and a root about size.

Pencil marks climb a kitchen doorframe, each one with a name and a date. Nobody saw the child get taller between the marks. It happened at night, at school, over cereal. Then one day the mark is above the parent's shoulder. In Hebrew, growing and great share a root. Gadal, he grew. Gadol, great, big. A gadol can be a grown-up, or a towering teacher. Being great and getting bigger are one family of words. Gimel, dalet, lamed: G-D-L.
screen: `MARKS ON A DOORFRAME.` → `GADAL: HE GREW.` → `G-D-L: GREAT, AND TO GROW.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the child. When Isaac, the long-awaited son, gets bigger, the Torah marks it simply: "And the child grew, and was weaned." And Abraham throws a great feast. The same root twice in one verse: the child grows, the feast is great. Growing is worth celebrating. Second, the promise: "I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and be thou a blessing." The sentence lands not on great, but on blessing. Some readers hear in it that being made great is for the sake of being a blessing. Third, the grown-up. Moses is raised in Pharaoh's palace, and then: "when Moses was grown up, that he went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens." What the grown Moses does is step outside and look at someone else's load. Growing up, in this verse, looks outward. Fourth, the prayer. The Kaddish, which you met on day six hundred three, opens with this root: yitgadal, may God's name grow great. Can God get bigger? Some teachers answer that it asks for God's greatness to grow in the world, in how people see and live. And mourners say it in a season when their own world may seem to have grown smaller. So G-D-L holds a child, a promise, a grown man and a prayer. In each, greatness isn't sitting still. It's growing, and pointed outward.
screen: `THE CHILD: AND THE CHILD GREW.` · `THE PROMISE: GREAT, TO BE A BLESSING.` · `THE GROWN-UP: HE LOOKED ON THEIR BURDENS.` · `THE PRAYER: YITGADAL.` · then, large: `גָּדַל`

segments.voice: Think of one thing in your reach that's growing, or trying to: a plant on a windowsill, a child learning to read, a new coworker finding their feet, a friendship that needs one more conversation. Picture the next small thing you could do for it, water, patience, a question, and imagine the next mark on the doorframe; if you pray, bring its name, or theirs, into the quiet. And if a loss is weighing on you today, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

Your line: grow. In Hebrew, great is something that is still growing. Until tomorrow, then.

1402.title: K-T-N
1402.howItsDone: Jewish teaching often turns to katan, small: the Talmud's story of the moon made smaller, Jacob's katonti, and the teaching in Pirkei Avot to treat a light commandment as carefully as a weighty one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, G-D-L: gadol, great, and the verb to grow. Your line was grow. Today, the root on the other side of the scale.

A prophet stands in a farmhouse in Bethlehem with a horn of oil, looking for a king. The farmer, Jesse, brings out his sons, one after another, tall ones, impressive ones. Each time the answer is no. Finally the prophet asks whether these are all the children. Jesse says, in effect, well, there's still the youngest, out with the sheep. In Hebrew he calls him ha-katan. The small one. Nobody thought to invite him. That small one is David.
screen: `A HORN OF OIL IN BETHLEHEM.` → `SEVEN SONS, ALL NO.` → `THERE'S STILL THE SMALL ONE.`

segments.voice: K-T-N. Kuf, tet, nun. Katan: small, little, young. First, the sky. Yesterday's root sits in Genesis next to today's: God made the two great lights, "the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night." The greater is gadol. The lesser is katan. A midrash in the Talmud tells that the moon objected to sharing the sky as an equal, and was told to make itself smaller. Then, the story goes, the moon was comforted: the righteous would be called by its name, David the small. So the small light and the small boy end up in the same story. Second, Jacob. On his way home, afraid of his brother, he prays, and the Hebrew has him say katonti, I am small, before all the kindness and truth God has shown him. A man with flocks and two camps of people, saying: I'm too small for all this. Third, the prophet Zechariah, watching a modest rebuilding that looked like nothing: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" The word for small things is from this root. Fourth, the street. In Jewish law, a katan is a minor, a child not yet obligated in the commandments. And the sayings of the fathers teach to be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, because you don't know the reward of each. Small doesn't mean it doesn't count. Small is often where it starts.

segments.voice: Look around for something small that does a job nobody thanks it for, a button, a hinge, a light switch, and rest your eyes on it for a few breaths. Then widen it to a person: someone easy to overlook in your day, whose name you may barely know, who keeps things running. If you pray, you can say a word of thanks for them.

1403.title: S-M-Ch
1403.howItsDone: Jews call a family celebration a simcha; on the festivals the joy is traditionally widened to include guests, the poor and the lonely, and on Simchat Torah the scrolls are carried around the synagogue with singing and dancing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, K-T-N: katan, small, the lesser light and the boy out with the sheep. Your line was small. You met festival joy and its guest list back on day five hundred; today, the root under it.

"Mazel tov, may we share in many more smachot." It's a line heard at bar mitzvahs, weddings, a baby naming, a family party with too much food. Smachot is the plural of simcha. In everyday Jewish English, a simcha isn't only a feeling. It's an event, with chairs and a caterer and an aunt who cries at the right moment. You don't usually have a simcha alone. And the Torah's instructions about joy come with a guest list.
screen: `MAY WE SHARE IN MANY SMACHOT.` → `A SIMCHA IS AN EVENT.` → `JOY WITH A GUEST LIST.`

segments.voice: S-M-Ch. Sin, mem, chet. Simcha: joy, gladness. Sameach: glad. And the verb, to rejoice. First, joy as a command. Deuteronomy, describing the harvest festival, says: "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast." It's in the same voice as the other instructions. Some readers ask: how do you command a feeling? One answer is that the Torah doesn't command the feeling. It commands the table, and the feeling tends to come and sit down. Second, the guest list. The same verse keeps going: thy son, and thy daughter, the servants, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. The festival joy is meant to reach people who have no table of their own. Maimonides, the medieval teacher, pressed the point hard. Someone who eats and drinks with family and locks the door against the poor and the bitter-hearted, he wrote, isn't rejoicing in a commandment. That's the joy of the stomach. Third, worship. A psalm sung in the morning prayers says: "Serve the LORD with gladness." The word for gladness is simcha. Fourth, the calendar. At the end of the fall festivals comes Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah, when the reading ends and begins again, and the scrolls are carried around the synagogue with dancing. Joy, in this root, is something you do, and something you do with people.

segments.voice: Let one good thing from the last few days come back, a message that made you laugh, good news, a meal better than it needed to be, and feel it again. Then picture one person who'd be glad to hear it, maybe someone a bit on their own lately, and hold their face in mind. If you pray, you can give thanks for the good thing.

1404.title: A-V-L
1404.howItsDone: Jewish mourners sit shiva, staying home after the burial while the community visits, brings food and makes up a prayer quorum; by custom visitors wait for the mourner to speak first, and on leaving they offer the traditional words of comfort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, S-M-Ch: simcha, joy with a guest list. Your line was joy. Job's silent friends first sat with you on day eight hundred forty; today, the root for the one they sat beside.

Three friends hear that a man named Job has lost everything: his animals, his servants, his children, and now his health. They set out from home and meet up to go to him together. From a distance they hardly recognize him. They weep, they tear their robes, they throw dust in the air. Then they do the thing the book remembers. They sit down with him on the ground, for seven days and seven nights, and nobody says a word. Later, they'll talk, and the talking won't go well. But the first week, they got exactly right.
screen: `THREE FRIENDS SET OUT.` → `THEY SIT ON THE GROUND.` → `SEVEN DAYS. NOT A WORD.`

segments.voice: A-V-L. Alef, vet, lamed. Avel: a mourner. Avelut: the time of mourning. First, a father in Genesis. Jacob's sons bring him their brother Joseph's coat, torn and bloodied, and he believes Joseph is dead. His children come to comfort him, and he won't be comforted. "For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning." Mourning there is avel: not a passing sadness, a state you live in. Second, Job's friends. The text says why they kept silent: "for they saw that his grief was very great." The rabbis turned that silence into a custom: visitors to a house of mourning wait for the mourner to speak first. You don't arrive with a speech. You arrive. Third, the shape of the time. The first week after a burial is shiva, from the word for seven. The mourners stay home, often sitting low, and the community comes to them, bringing food and filling the room so the prayers can be said there. Then the mourning loosens in stages, over the following weeks and the year. Grief isn't told to be over by a date. It's given rooms to move through. Fourth, the comforters' words. When visitors leave a house of mourning, the traditional line asks that God comfort the mourner among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. Even the comfort puts the mourner inside a larger group. An avel is someone the community is holding up.
screen: `JACOB: I WILL GO DOWN MOURNING.` · `JOB'S FRIENDS: SILENCE FIRST.` · `SHIVA: THE COMMUNITY COMES TO YOU.` · `AMONG THE MOURNERS OF ZION.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T SPEAK. YOU ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is grieving, recently or years ago, and simply sit with them in your mind, the way Job's friends sat on the ground; you don't have to fix it or find words. If you're the one mourning, let yourself be sat with, and if you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If grief ever feels like too much to carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

1405.title: Sh-K-N
1405.hook: Shechinah, mishkan and shachen, neighbor: presence is neighborly
1405.howItsDone: Jews speak of the Shechinah, God's indwelling presence, resting where people gather to pray and study; the same root gives mishkan, the wilderness sanctuary, and shachen, a neighbor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-V-L: avel, the mourner, and friends who sat on the ground without a word. Your line was mourning. You met the Shechinah on day one thousand one hundred eighty; today, the root it grows from.

"Better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off." That's Proverbs, and it's blunt. A brother may love you dearly. But if he lives three states away, the one with the spare key, who notices when the mail piles up, is the person next door. The Hebrew for that neighbor is shachen: the one who dwells near. Hold that word, because the same three letters turn up somewhere you wouldn't expect: in the Torah's word for the place God's presence lives, and in the rabbis' word for the presence itself.
screen: `A NEIGHBOR NEAR, A BROTHER FAR.` → `SHACHEN: THE ONE WHO DWELLS NEAR.` → `THE SAME LETTERS, SOMEWHERE ELSE.`

segments.voice: Sh-K-N. Shin, kaf, nun. The verb shachan: to dwell, to settle, to live somewhere. First, the tent. In the wilderness, God tells Moses: "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them." Dwell is shachanti, from this root. The tent they build is the mishkan, the dwelling place, the portable sanctuary carried from camp to camp. Notice the verse: not that I may dwell in it. Among them. The tent is the address; the people are the neighborhood. Second, the presence. The rabbis gave God's nearness a name: the Shechinah, the indwelling, the presence that settles. In the sayings of the fathers, a teacher says that when ten sit together and study Torah, the Shechinah rests among them, and the text goes further: even two, even one. Third, the neighbor. Shachen shares its letters with mishkan and Shechinah; dictionaries list them under one root. Whether a teacher means anything by it is up to the reader. But some readers hear it: the word for God's presence and the word for the person next door are built the same way. So in this root, presence isn't a light in the sky. It's someone who lives close, who stays, who can be knocked on.
screen: `THAT I MAY DWELL AMONG THEM.` · `MISHKAN: THE DWELLING PLACE.` · `SHECHINAH: THE PRESENCE THAT SETTLES.` · `SHACHEN: THE NEIGHBOR.` · then, large: `PRESENCE IS NEIGHBORLY.`

segments.voice: Picture the people who live closest to you, through the wall, across the hall, down the road, some known by name and some only by their dog or the sound of their door. Let each come to mind for a breath, then rest on one household and think of one neighborly thing that would suit them. If you pray, you can hold that household in your prayer.

1406.title: K-H-L
1406.hook: kahal, kehillah: an assembly, a community
1406.howItsDone: Jewish communities are often called kehillot, and Jewish life gathers people for prayer, learning and the life cycle; some communities hold a hakhel gathering in the year after the sabbatical year, recalling Deuteronomy 31.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-K-N: the mishkan, the Shechinah, and shachen, the neighbor. Your line was presence is neighborly. On day three hundred sixty-eight, Moses gathered everyone after the golden calf; today, the root of that gathering.

There's a book in the Bible whose author doesn't give a name, just a title: Kohelet. It opens with a man looking hard at life and calling all of it vapor, breath, here and gone. English Bibles call the book Ecclesiastes, and the speaker the Preacher. But Kohelet comes from a root that means to gather a crowd: something like the Gatherer, or the one who speaks to the assembly. A book this lonely-sounding is named for a crowd.
screen: `A BOOK WITH A TITLE, NOT A NAME.` → `KOHELET: THE GATHERER.` → `NAMED FOR A CROWD.`

segments.voice: K-H-L. Kuf, hey, lamed. Kahal: an assembly, a congregation. Kehillah: a community. And the verb, to gather people together. First, the great gathering. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses gives an instruction for the festival of booths, once every seven years: read the teaching aloud to everyone. Look who's on the list: "Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and thy stranger that is within thy gates." Not the leaders, not the scholars: the whole crowd, kids and newcomer included, so that, the verse says, they may hear and learn. The rabbis called this gathering hakhel: gather. Second, the community that lasts. For centuries, a Jewish town's organized community, with its synagogue, its burial society, its charity fund, its school, was called a kehillah. It's the people who show up for a wedding, a shiva house, a bris, a sick neighbor. Some congregations still use the word in their names. Third, the warning. In the sayings of the fathers, Hillel teaches: don't separate yourself from the community. Hillel's word there is a different one, tzibbur, but the point lands on kehillah. You can learn alone, and pray alone, but the tradition keeps pulling you back toward the room full of other people. Even Kohelet, with his big questions, takes his name from the crowd he spoke them to.
screen: `KAHAL: THE ASSEMBLY.` · `GATHER MEN, WOMEN, CHILDREN, STRANGER.` · `KEHILLAH: THE COMMUNITY THAT SHOWS UP.` · `DON'T SEPARATE YOURSELF.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE CROWD.`

segments.voice: Let your circles come to mind as rooms full of faces: family, friends, coworkers, a class, a street, a congregation, and notice one that hasn't gathered in a while. Picture them at one table, then add someone usually left off the list, the newcomer, the stranger within your gates. If you pray, you can hold that circle in your prayer.

1407.title: A-Ch-D
1407.hook: echad, one, as in the Shema
1407.howItsDone: Jews say the Shema morning and evening, traditionally covering the eyes for the first line and lingering on its last word, echad, with the intention that God is one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, K-H-L: kahal and kehillah, the whole crowd gathered, the kids and the stranger too. Your line was community. The Shema has been with you since day thirteen; today, the end of the week, and its last word.

The first chapter of Genesis counts the days of creation. Day two, a second day. Day three, a third. But the first one isn't called the first. In the Hebrew, after the light and the dark, the verse says: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Not first. One. The commentator Rashi noticed it and gave a reason: on that day God was alone, the only one in the world. Ordinal numbers come later. On day one there is only one.
screen: `DAY TWO, DAY THREE...` → `BUT NOT THE FIRST DAY.` → `ONE DAY.`

segments.voice: A-Ch-D. Alef, chet, dalet. Echad: one. First, the Shema, the line said morning and night, and at the end of a life: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Echad is its last word. The Talmud says that whoever draws out the word echad has their days drawn out. So the custom is to linger on it, especially the last letter, and in that pause to let God's oneness fill everything: heaven, earth, and the four directions. Second, people. In Genesis, a couple becomes basar echad, one flesh. At Sinai, a teaching of the rabbis says, the people camped facing the mountain like one person with one heart. Echad isn't only a number. It's the word for many becoming whole. Third, this week. It began with G-D-L, great and growing. Then K-T-N, the small one in the field. S-M-Ch, joy with a guest list. A-V-L, the mourner, and friends who sat in silence. Sh-K-N, the presence that dwells with the neighbors. K-H-L, the crowd gathered to hear. Great and small, joy and grief, neighbor and crowd. The same Shema is said on a wedding morning and in a shiva house, by the tallest and the smallest voice in the room. One isn't the opposite of many. One is what many can become.
screen: `THE LAST WORD OF THE SHEMA.` · `LINGER ON ECHAD.` · `ONE FLESH, ONE HEART.` · `THE WEEK: GREAT, SMALL, JOY, GRIEF, NEIGHBOR, CROWD.` · then, large: `ONE.`

segments.voice: For a few minutes, choose one thing only, your breath, the sounds of the room or the feel of your hands, and when a second thing starts, a list, a worry, a plan, notice it and come back to the one, no scolding. If you pray, you can say the Shema slowly and stay a while on its last word, the way the custom lingers on echad; if you don't, simply breathe out long on the word one.
screen: `CHOOSE ONE THING.` · `NOTICE THE SECOND.` · `COME BACK TO ONE.`
